docs.text: Session 19: Thunder, Ale, and the Dragon's Answer The party returned to Bremen with Spellix Romwood in tow, the Shield Guardian stomping along behind them — its iron frame still covered head to toe in goblin graffiti. Spellix thanked them with genuine warmth, explained he would be staying at the inn briefly before heading south to his family, then turned out his pockets to reveal they were entirely empty. He shrugged. Perhaps the inn was too much to hope for. Aronious pressed two gold into his hand without a word. Rest, at least, would come easy. Dzaan was sent ahead to the inn as well. He walked through the door, sat down at the nearest table, and immediately began scrawling in his spellbook with the focused desperation of a man racing against his own memory. He did not look up. Yin Shen remarked that it was past time they all rested — everyone had taken a beating. Hobbins and Aronious turned to look at her with the flat, unified expression of two people covered in bruises regarding someone without a single mark on them. Yin Shen said nothing further. Before rest could be considered, Hobbins had unfinished business. The Shield Guardian stood in the street where they had left it, patient and enormous and absolutely covered in goblin scrawl. She was not willing to leave it that way. The party browsed the shelves of the local market, where they found a bottle of Grizwald's Famous Degreaser with the tagline: It'll remove anything and everything. The clerk admitted, without any apparent shame, that it was in fact terrible at removing grease but cut through paint as though it had never existed. Too harsh. They put it back. Instead they selected green, pink, purple, and black paint and a set of brushes, and set about the rather more delicate work of making the construct look less like a siege weapon and more like something a person might not immediately flee from. Hobbins applied the finishing touch herself: a pink peace symbol, carefully painted across the Guardian's forehead. It helped. Somewhat. Yin Shen suggested, again, that they head inside to rest. Aronious made only a token effort to stop Hobbins from lunging at Yin Shen's ankles, his grip conspicuously loose as the ferret squeaked about not a single arrow having touched her, about bruises, about the Shield Guardian nearly being destroyed. The scuffle resolved itself in time, and the party made for their rooms. They had barely started up the stairs when the door burst open. Mylbor Tarrfak filled the frame, crimson-stained sack slung over one shoulder and Thunder Stick raised in one hand — or what remained of it. The end had mushroomed outward into a tangle of singed and curling metal. He grinned the grin of a man who had fired his only shot and found it sufficient. "Only took one shot," he said, dropping the sack on the floor with a wet thud. "Though I only had one shot." A hearty laugh filled the room. He threw his coin purse onto the bar before anyone could object, ordered a round, and passed tankards to Yin Shen and Aronious. Aronious, with careful deliberation, poured a bottle cap's worth of clear liquor for Hobbins. They raised their drinks. Mylbor drained his in a single pull and looked around the table with the expectant expression of a man waiting to be matched. Aronious, reasoning that a sufficiently drunk Mylbor might prove a more cooperative ally, accepted the implied challenge. He seized a full bottle of clear liquor and poured it down without pause. Mylbor turned to the barmaid and asked what that equated to in ale. She said a full cask. Mylbor's eyes lit up. He was already behind the bar and on the floor before anyone thought to stop him. Yin Shen grabbed the handle of the keg and opened it. Mylbor sputtered, drank, gulped, and sputtered again — and eventually, with great reluctance, tapped the floor. He stood slowly, thumped his chest, and produced a belch of considerable authority. "You win, laddy." Yin Shen suggested it was time for everyone to sleep. Hobbins, no longer able to contain herself on the subject of Yin Shen's perfect, unmarked, unscathed person, launched herself across the room. The scuffle was brief. Things settled. The party went to bed. They rose early, waited for Mylbor to surface, and found him in reasonable shape for a man who had consumed a cask of ale. Over breakfast, he and Yin Shen came to an agreement: they would stay in contact. She wanted word of the ancient white dragon that roamed Icewind Dale. He wanted word of anything worth hunting. Both parties shook on it and parted ways. The road to Termalaine ate most of the day, and the party arrived in the evening to find a large orc in fine clothing standing in the street barking orders at a cluster of civilians doing their best impression of a town militia. Most of them looked as though they had never held a weapon before last week. He turned when the party approached. They explained they were working under Captain Imdra Arlaggath and were looking for the town Speaker. "You've found him," he said, and introduced himself as Oarus Masthew . Imdra's warning had reached him, and he had wasted no time. Every able-bodied person in Termalaine who could hold a spear was now, in some technical sense, a soldier. The party left him to it. Finding a quiet corner to think, the group turned to a question that had been waiting long enough: the ancient white dragon. Yin Shen was confident. White dragons, she explained, were benevolent creatures. They enjoyed the company of people. Hobbins composed herself, reached for the magic of sending , and pushed the message outward into the cold. "Don't panic, we are friendly, need help, Ten-Towns in danger, meet at Redwaters, Lupine can vouch, at sundown in two days. Ciao!" The answer came back low and rasping, like stone grinding against stone. "Come to my lair at the Sea of Moving Ice. You'll find a shipwreck I use as one of my homes." Two days of travel, at minimum. The direction was vague. The invitation was not the kind one declined. As they moved through Termalaine's streets turning the logistics over in their minds, a posting on the Gelp board stopped them short. Written in urgent, uneven letters: Miners Lost! 50g Reward. Below it, in smaller text, a note that the local miners' guild had refused all work until the lost men were found and the mine declared safe. Fifty gold was fifty gold. They looked at one another, looked at the road stretching north toward the Sea of Moving Ice, and thought about it for a longer moment than any of them would readily admit. The dragon was waiting. They turned up their collars and walked back out into the cold.

docs.text: Session 2: The Many Whispers in Easthaven When the travelers returned to the Trail's End Tavern , the night was calm and cold, and the road behind them lay silent. Yet one thing was amiss — Torg's Company was gone, their sleds and dogs no where to be seen. Left while the part was away. As they pondered their next course, the tavern door opened, letting in a gust of frost and a figure robed in rusty brown and red — Dzaan . His eyes sparkled with curiosity rather than menace, and a hint of a smile tugged at his lips. “Adventurers, by the look of you,” he said, striding to their table. “I’m conducting research on the elemental spirits that dwell in this land — Chwingas , I believe the locals call them. Elusive little things. I would pay handsomely for their study.” Behind him, a companion in studded leather lingered at the doorway, but before the group could take a good look, the door shut and the figure was gone. Dzaan placed a small lantern of gentle blue fire upon the table. “This,” he explained, “is attuned to the spirits. It glows when they are near. Bring me one, and twenty-five gold is yours.” Hobbins' eager chatter — and Yin Shen's foxlike grin — saw the wizard laugh and raise the offer. “A fine bit of negotiation,” he admitted, “and a sign of capable company. Thirty gold pieces it is.” The party accepted and returned to the forest, lantern in hand. There, beneath the whispering pines, they sought to coax the Chwingas from hiding. Remembering the tales that the spirits were fond of childish wonder, the group began to dance, sing, and play at circles in the snow — ring around the rosy beneath the moonlight. It was a comical sight: Aronious trying, with some dignity, to keep pace; Yin Shen spinning with genuine delight; and Hobbins darting through the snow like a ribbon of fur and laughter. Yet for all their effort, no spirit appeared. The lantern’s flame flickered once, then stilled. With frost clinging to their cloaks and little gained for their play, they decided to continue their travels east to Easthaven . By the time they arrived, the sky was black and heavy with snow. The lamps of The White Lady Inn shone dimly through the storm — a welcome sight. Inside, warmth and music greeted them, and a bard named Rinaldo was making his rounds, filling the room with song and stories of the inn’s spectral namesake. The trio took their rest there. The next day as they warmed themselves by the hearth, a bard named Rinaldo approached — a man of quick fingers and quicker tongue — proclaiming that he would hold a séance to summon the spirit of the inn’s namesake, the White Lady who drowned long ago beneath the frozen lake. Yin Shen ventured into the square, where she stumbled upon a grim spectacle — Dzaan , the very wizard who had so warmly hired them, bound to a stake as the townsfolk gathered round. The flames climbed swiftly, and he met his end with unsettling calm. Beside Yin Shen stood Captain Imdra Arlaggath , the stern leader of Easthaven’s guard. Seeing her disquiet, the captain muttered, “Do not pity him, stranger. He murdered those he hired — folk of Icewind Dale — after they aided his travels. He’s reaping what he sowed.” When the captain turned her questioning gaze to Yin Shen , the rogue answered plainly that she and her companions had only crossed Dzaan’s path briefly, and were in fact hunting Sephek Kaltro , the killer who had plagued Ten-Towns. Hearing that the murderer was no more, the captain’s demeanor softened. “You’ve a sharp eye and a steady hand,” she said. “We’ve fishermen gone missing out on the ice. Find them, and what Dzaan carried in life shall be yours in death.” The reward, as it turned out, included a Scroll of Fireball and a curious Gray Bag of Tricks , both lightly scorched from the pyre. Meanwhile, Aronious and Hobbins visited The Wet Trout , a lively and unruly tavern favored by miners and sailors. docs.text: Session 20: The White and the Wanderer The party struck out from Termalaine into the open wilderness, the dogsled cutting fresh tracks through unmarked snow. The Sea of Moving Ice lay somewhere ahead — how far, exactly, was a question the landscape declined to answer. They traveled through the full length of the day until the dogs began to labor and the light bled out of the sky, then made camp in the lee of a low ridge and settled in for a cold night. Yin Shen took first watch. The camp was quiet. The wind pressed low across the tundra and the dogs curled into one another for warmth. Then Dzaan lurched upright from his bedroll with the sudden, breathless energy of a man surfacing from drowning. He was already moving before Yin Shen could speak. His hands swept through the snow in long deliberate strokes, carving lines and angles into the frozen ground — a teleportation circle, drawn freehand and fast, the geometry of it precise in a way that suggested the pattern lived somewhere deep in his hands rather than in his waking mind. His words came in a tangle. Red Wizards of Thay. Here in Ten-Towns. Looking for him. He could not say how they had found him or how long he had before they did, only that if they found him alongside the party, the party became a problem they would also need to solve. He would not allow that. Yin Shen asked about the magic training he had promised her. He stopped. For a moment the frantic energy went still. Then, without hesitation, he reached into his coat and produced a small folio — handwritten, tight script filling every margin — and pressed it into her hands. "Keep practicing," he said. He tried to smile. It almost worked. Arcane light gathered between his palms. The circle blazed blue-white against the snow, and then he was gone. The lines faded. The snow settled back into the shape of the tundra as though nothing had been drawn there at all. When the others woke and the disappearance was discussed, the party was quiet for a moment. Then they broke camp, and Aronious took watch while the rest settled back in. He was leaning against a rock, scanning the dark, when something jabbed him sharply in the ribs. He looked down. A Chwinga stood at his side — tiny, bright-eyed, trembling with barely contained delight at its own audacity. When Aronious did not immediately shout or swat at it, the creature dissolved into a fit of tinkling laughter. He played along. They sat together in the cold for a while, the ranger and the small elemental spirit, occupying the same patch of dark in the way that two very different creatures sometimes find themselves briefly sharing the same world. Eventually the Chwinga darted behind the rock. It reappeared a moment later carrying a snowflake — enormous relative to its small frame, pristine and many-pointed, glimmering faintly with something that was not quite ordinary light. With great ceremony, it pressed the charm into Aronious's hand. Then it turned, retrieved two more charms from the ground behind the rock, and set them carefully where Hobbins and Yin Shen would find them in the morning. It looked back at Aronious once — a look that seemed to say that was entirely the plan all along — and disappeared. By the time the dogs were rested and the party was moving again, the landscape had changed. The ground grew harder, the air sharper, and the horizon began to show the grey-white suggestion of pack ice. The Sea of Moving Ice announced itself gradually and then all at once — a frozen expanse broken by pressure ridges and deep blue fissures, stretching away into a sky that seemed to press down rather than lift. The shipwreck was not difficult to find. Its hull rose from the ice at a list, half-consumed by the freeze, every timber grey and salt-stripped. The hull had been opened — not by rot, not by weather, but by something that had simply decided a wall was an inconvenience. The edges of the breach were smooth in a way that suggested size and indifference in equal measure. From inside came a rhythmic, bestial hammering. The party exchanged a look and went in anyway. The frost troll filled the hold the way a storm fills a valley — completely, and with a sense that it had been there longer than anything else. It came for them without preamble, talons and teeth leading, its pale bulk terrifyingly fast in the confined dark. What followed was close and brutal. Aronious put arrows into it from every angle he could find. Yin Shen moved through the shadows between its strikes with the economy of someone who understood that a single clean hit mattered more than volume. Hobbins hurled spells with reckless precision, reading the creature's regeneration and understanding, with a wizard's cold clarity, that cold would not save them here. She switched to fire. The troll's flesh stopped knitting. Its movements grew ragged. And when the moment arrived, the Shield Guardian settled the matter with characteristic efficiency — punching straight through the rotten hull as though the timber were parchment, then punching the troll so hard it left the ground entirely and met the far wall at considerable speed. The fire Hobbins had already set in its flesh did the rest. It did not get up. The hold creaked and settled around them. Beneath the ice, the dragon's hoard glimmered. The party began stacking rotten wood to build a fire, hoping to melt enough of the freeze to reach it. While the fire took hold, Yin Shen explored the hold's deeper compartments. A barricaded door at the far end had clearly been what the troll was hammering against. She opened it. Four kobolds stared back at her. They were disheveled but intact, and — notably — they did not attack. The party asked about the dragon. The kobolds confirmed they served it. The party asked if the dragon was friendly toward Ten-Towns. The kobolds found this so genuinely funny that two of them had to sit down. The party began to deliberate. Hobbins sent periodic fire bolts skyward — makeshift flares punching bright orange against the grey — while Aronious did the same with flaming arrows. They waited. The dragon arrived the way weather arrives: not all at once, but with a building pressure that preceded it by some margin. Thunderous wingbeats. The crack of ice giving way. A shadow moving across the ship's hull that was larger than the hull itself. Then a voice — low, resonant, and terribly pleased with itself. "Ahh. I smell the tender flesh and hear the panicked heartbeat of the meal that so eagerly delivered itself to me." The kobolds immediately burst into laughter and fled into the darkest corners they could find. The party pressed into the shadows. As the dragon's great serpentine head pushed through the breach, they saw its eyes — filmed over, pale and clouded. The creature was ancient enough that its sight had largely failed it. It was hunting by smell and sound. Then a voice from outside, calm and almost conversational: "I think you could use some help." An incantation. A fog cloud rolled through the hold in a single dense surge, swallowing everything. "To me!" They ran toward the voice. They emerged from the ship into the open ice to find a figure standing in the fog — nine feet tall, broad as a doorway, wrapped in walrus pelts, with a club and shield already being shouldered into carry position. She did not wait for introductions. "Quick. My cave." They ran. Behind them the dragon's howl split the air with a fury that was equal parts hunger and insult, and it answered its own anger with a blast of breath aimed at the sky. Spears of ice came down from above like thrown lances, slamming into the frozen ground in a tight and terrible rain. One landed close enough to Hobbins to throw her forward off her feet. Yin Shen caught her without breaking stride and kept moving. Aronious went down twice on the broken ice, and twice Yin Shen found him, pulled him upright, and shoved him forward. They hit the cave entrance at a run and kept going until the stone closed around them and the sound of the dragon faded to a distant, furious echo. The giant set her club and shield against the cave wall with the unhurried manner of someone returning from an unremarkable errand. As she straightened, she passed close to a low rock shelf, and a small shape emerged from the shadow behind it — a Chwinga , its face marked with a pattern that felt immediately, inexplicably familiar. It reached up. The giant extended her little finger, and the creature touched it gently. A greeting. Old and certain, between two beings who had known each other for some time. The party stood in the cave mouth, breathing hard, and said nothing for a moment. Outside, ice continued to fall.

docs.text: Session 21: The Mines of Termalaine The giant's name was Tinjong , and she filled her cave the way certain people fill a room — not through effort, but through simple fact of presence. She was a Verbeeg, she explained, and a servant of Sylvanas, god of nature. The fight between Ten-Towns and the Duergar was not her concern, and she made no apology for that. But the Rime was another matter. An endless, unnatural winter pressed against the grain of the world itself, and anything that moved against Auril could count on her when the time came. Aronious spent some time in quiet conversation with her — the particular kind of exchange that passes between two people who understand the wild and are not in a hurry. Eventually the party took their leave, the cave and the crashing ice and the distant anger of a dragon falling away behind them as they pointed the dogsled back toward Termalaine . The Gelp board had turned over since they had last looked at it. New postings, new complaints, new requests filling the space where others had silently vanished. But one notice remained exactly where it had been, patient and unchanged: Miners Lost! 50g Reward. Below it, the note about the guild's refusal to work until the mines were cleared. They found the mining offices without trouble and the man behind the desk without ceremony. Foreman Lancastor was a gruff, direct human who said what he meant and did not appear to own a great deal of patience for anything else. The situation, as he laid it out, was simple: miners were missing, kobolds had moved in, and no one on his crew was going back down until something was done about it. The party headed for the mines. A sign had been posted at the entrance in handwriting far too precise and deliberate to belong to any miner: NO ENTRY — KOBOLDS ONLY. The party went in anyway. The upper tunnels rewarded careful attention. A few gemstones came loose from the walls with some patient work, and the signs of kobold habitation grew denser the deeper they went — scratched markings, scattered debris, the particular smell of something small and numerous living somewhere in the dark. They found the central shaft without warning. It dropped away into nothing, a pit with no apparent bottom, a waterfall somewhere below filling the silence with white noise. A narrow wooden walkway traced the edge of the shaft, more suggestion than structure. Hobbins pressed herself to the planks and listened. Beneath the waterfall's roar she caught something else — rhythmic, deliberate. Sawing. She peered over the edge. Two kobolds clung to the walkway's supports below, working their blades through the timber with focused industry. Hobbins didn't deliberate. She cast thunderwave downward with both paws. The kobolds disappeared into the shaft. The sawing stopped. Deeper still, the tunnels opened into a chamber where gemstones caught the light from the walls in clusters of cold color. Hobbins moved to examine them, found one that looked promising, and began working at it with her knife. Something descended from the ceiling without sound. The Grell was on them before anyone had properly registered it — a bulbous, tentacled horror that had apparently decided the chamber was its own. It did not remain that opinion for long. The party dispatched it with the efficient aggression of a group that had stopped being surprised by things dropping from above, and pressed onward. A crack in the stone at the tunnel's far end opened onto a cramped space where more kobolds had made themselves at home. The party approached without weapons drawn. One kobold did the talking. It stepped forward ahead of the others and spoke — clearly, fluently, with a precision that sat entirely wrong in a kobold's mouth. Its wings, on closer inspection, were not real. It wore them. Something was off about it in ways that went beyond vocabulary. The party pressed. Intimidation opened what conversation had not. The kobold was possessed — something riding behind its eyes and speaking through its throat. Before it could recover itself, Hobbins' hand darted out and came away with a dirty pouch from its belt. She walked to the edge of the central shaft and dropped it in. The ghost erupted from the kobold like steam from a wound, shrieking, and plunged after the pouch into the dark below. The kobold swayed, blinked, and looked around at the tunnel with the bewildered expression of someone who had just woken up somewhere unexpected. What remained of the conversation was considerably more straightforward. The kobolds, freed of whatever had been steering them, turned out to want very little — warmth, food, and somewhere to be that wasn't a frozen mine shaft. They had no particular attachment to the life of banditry they had apparently been directed into. Yin Shen offered them a deal: work the mines for Termalaine, free of charge, in exchange for meals and lodging in town. The kobolds agreed with an enthusiasm that suggested they had not been offered anything resembling a fair arrangement in some time. There remained the question of getting three kobolds through a town without incident. Yin Shen pulled a blanket from her pack and tossed it over. She explained, briefly, the general shape of the plan: get to the foreman, let the party do the talking, stay under the blanket. The kobolds conferred. Then, with great seriousness of purpose, two of them crouched and one climbed atop the others' shoulders. The topmost tied the blanket around itself like a hooded cloak. The resulting silhouette stood in the torchlight — compact, lopsided, and swaying slightly at the joints. A reasonable person, in poor light, at some distance, might almost have mistaken it for a dragonborn. They set off toward town.

Hobbins moved to examine them, found one that looked promising, and began working at it with her knife. Something descended from the ceiling without sound. The Grell was on them before anyone had properly registered it — a bulbous, tentacled horror that had apparently decided the chamber was its own. It did not remain that opinion for long. The party dispatched it with the efficient aggression of a group that had stopped being surprised by things dropping from above, and pressed onward. A crack in the stone at the tunnel's far end opened onto a cramped space where more kobolds had made themselves at home. The party approached without weapons drawn. One kobold did the talking. It stepped forward ahead of the others and spoke — clearly, fluently, with a precision that sat entirely wrong in a kobold's mouth. Its wings, on closer inspection, were not real. It wore them. Something was off about it in ways that went beyond vocabulary. The party pressed. Intimidation opened what conversation had not. The kobold was possessed — something riding behind its eyes and speaking through its throat. Before it could recover itself, Hobbins' hand darted out and came away with a dirty pouch from its belt. She walked to the edge of the central shaft and dropped it in. The ghost erupted from the kobold like steam from a wound, shrieking, and plunged after the pouch into the dark below. The kobold swayed, blinked, and looked around at the tunnel with the bewildered expression of someone who had just woken up somewhere unexpected. What remained of the conversation was considerably more straightforward. The kobolds, freed of whatever had been steering them, turned out to want very little — warmth, food, and somewhere to be that wasn't a frozen mine shaft. They had no particular attachment to the life of banditry they had apparently been directed into. Yin Shen offered them a deal: work the mines for Termalaine, free of charge, in exchange for meals and lodging in town. The kobolds agreed with an enthusiasm that suggested they had not been offered anything resembling a fair arrangement in some time. There remained the question of getting three kobolds through a town without incident. Yin Shen pulled a blanket from her pack and tossed it over. She explained, briefly, the general shape of the plan: get to the foreman, let the party do the talking, stay under the blanket. The kobolds conferred. Then, with great seriousness of purpose, two of them crouched and one climbed atop the others' shoulders. The topmost tied the blanket around itself like a hooded cloak. The resulting silhouette stood in the torchlight — compact, lopsided, and swaying slightly at the joints. A reasonable person, in poor light, at some distance, might almost have mistaken it for a dragonborn. They set off toward town.
docs.title: Session 21: The Mines of Termalaine

docs.text: Session 22: The Fortress in the Spine Foreman Lancastor looked at the three kobolds for a long time. Then he said he needed to check with the Speaker first, and left the room with the expression of a man buying himself time to think. He returned with Oarus Masthew , who looked at the kobolds, looked at the party, and formally accepted the arrangement on behalf of Termalaine without visible hesitation. Food and shelter in exchange for work in the mines. The kobolds, still under the blanket, swayed slightly with what appeared to be restrained excitement. Masthew asked the party to follow him to the town hall. His expression, once the door closed behind them, had changed. Imdra had been taken. Easthaven had been hit — hard, fast, and with purpose. Termalaine had repelled its own incursion and, in doing so, had captured a Duergar. Under questioning, he had given up the location of the stronghold. Deep in the mountains. The Spine of the World . The party left the town hall with more to carry than they had walked in with. Yin Shen had unfinished business first. She found the armorer — a dragonborn named Karthax — and laid the Grell tentacles on his workbench. He turned them over, considered the tensile quality of the tissue, and told her to return in the morning. She also found the mine's own appraiser, a wiry, balding man with a nasal voice who handled the gemstone she had pried from the tunnel wall as though it were something personal. His astonishment was genuine. He put the value close to a hundred gold and made no secret of wanting to buy it. Yin Shen pocketed the stone and left. In the morning, Karthax presented his work: the tentacles had been cured and lashed with leather bindings into a serviceable whip. Yin Shen took it without ceremony. Hobbins reached for her sending spell and pushed a message toward Mylbor Tarrfak . Duergar. Stronghold. Come now. His answer came back in the same register it always did — immediate and enthusiastic. He arrived that evening, kicking the inn door open ahead of himself and announcing his presence to the room at considerable volume. They took the Eastway east at pace. Passing Easthaven , they saw what had been done to it. The great front gate was blackened by fire and split by some force that had not bothered to find a seam — raw, purposeful destruction left half-repaired in the cold. The party did not slow. They redoubled instead. Aronious guided them up into the mountains with a ranger's instinct, reading the terrain and steering them clear of the worst of it — the hidden drops, the unstable slopes, the places where the snow moved. They climbed until the foothills gave way to the raw stone of the Spine itself, and the stronghold rose above them without warning: sheer walls carved directly from the mountain's body, arrowslits running its face in rows and glowing faintly from within. A narrow stair slicked with ice ran up along the side to a single large stone door. They approached. From somewhere within came the sound of a lock disengaging. The door had not been opened for them. It had been set. The crossbow bolt came through the arrowslit the moment they stepped inside. Nine Duergar stationed in the barracks flanking the entrance were already on their feet, already enlarging, filling the narrow entrance hall with grey iron bulk. The space gave nothing away — too tight for half the party to find a useful angle, Mylbor and Polard pressed against the walls with nowhere to bring their considerable capacity to bear. Hobbins made the space work anyway. Her chromatic orbs ricocheted through the hall in bursts of elemental fury, each one carrying its damage from one grey body to the next. Aronious sent arrows back through the arrowslit with careful economy while directing the Shield Guardian into the doorway as a wall of iron, plugging the corridor against the Duergar's numbers. Yin Shen scattered caltrops across the threshold and waited. Every Duergar who tried to advance paid for the attempt. When the hall went quiet, they moved on. An adjacent chamber held a table — not a table exactly, but a map carved in relief from solid stone. Ten-Towns rendered in precise, miniature detail, the surrounding wilderness etched down to individual ridgelines. A channel had been cut through the carving, running between all ten settlements in a continuous loop, and suspended on an iron pole within it sat a dragon figurine. A crank on the side moved it. The party turned it and watched the dragon trace its circuit through the towns without a word. Beyond the map room, a large ornate bed and a chest at its foot marked someone's private quarters. Yin Shen had the lock open before anyone suggested caution. The chest held gem-encrusted garments. She had them out and distributed before anyone suggested patience. A hatch in the bottom triggered as the last item cleared the chest. Poison gas flooded the room. Hobbins hit the door and held it. On the other side, Yin Shen hammered. Aronious tried to pull Hobbins clear by main force and she shook him off without looking. It took Yin Shen's voice, then Aronious's, then Polard's — all three of them, in sequence — before Hobbins finally released the door. Yin Shen came through gasping. She went down onto the stone floor and did not move for some time. The party waited. A small closet hidden off the map room held what the chest had not: several mind flayer skulls arranged around a chardalyn statuette at the center. Hobbins put a crossbow bolt through it without preamble. It shattered across the floor. Yin Shen reached out and touched one of the skulls. She did not move. Her hand remained extended, one finger barely grazing the bone, and she stood perfectly still while the rest of the party watched. To them, nothing happened. To Yin Shen, time was moving — days, then weeks, then longer, an accelerating pull dragging her northward through years and then ages, her body fixed in place while something vast and cold unwound around her. Aronious and Hobbins pulled her hand clear of the skull. She came back without warning, the way a candle relights — all at once, no gradual return. Unharmed. She looked at the skull for a moment and said nothing. They turned back to the map table. The dragon figurine sat in its channel, waiting to be moved. The channel connecting all ten towns, the iron pole, the crank — all of it patient and precise, a plan laid out in miniature. Someone had been plotting the route for a long time.

docs.text: Session 23: The Heart of Sunblight The western hallway led them to a door, and the door led them to something none of them had expected. The woman inside was old in the way that certain things are old — not diminished by it, but concentrated. Long black hair shot through with ribbons of white fell past her shoulders, and her fingernails curved like shards of dark iron. Before her spread a hearty buffet of cooked meats, mushrooms, and stranger fare from deeper places that none of the party cared to identify. She looked up when the door opened, assessed them in a single sweep, and gestured to the empty chairs at her table. Her guards received a different signal. Weapons away. Back to cooking. Hobbins sat down and, in the spirit of diplomacy, forced a single bite of something past her lips. She excused herself from the room with as much dignity as the situation allowed and returned somewhat paler. The woman introduced herself as Grandolpha Muzgardt — paramour of Xardorok Sunblight , the Duergar lord whose fortress they were currently standing inside. She said it without embarrassment, and what followed explained why. She had no allegiance to him worth the name. For some time she had been working from within his command, quietly pulling Duergar loyalties toward herself and away from his ambitions. Her intention, once the ground was ready, was to withdraw entirely — to take her people back into the Underdark and breathe life into the failing realm Xardorok had abandoned when the surface offered him grander dreams of conquest. She was not an ally by any warm definition of the word. But her interests and theirs pointed, for the moment, in the same direction. The party asked if her guards could arrange a shift change — enough cover to get them into the lower levels and find Imdra before Xardorok knew anyone was looking. Grandolpha agreed, and they made a plan. Her men would escort the party in as though they belonged there. From the prison cells, the rest would follow. The shift change moved them through a service elevator and into the lower stronghold, past a cluster of throne room guards bearing Xardorok's sigil who refused the unscheduled rotation without a word and without moving. Grandolpha's escort navigated around them with the practiced ease of people accustomed to working inside a command structure while quietly subverting it. They were brought through the main forge. The ceiling ranged forty feet at its peak and pressed down to twenty along the southern wall, the whole cavern swimming in heat and smoke. At its center stood a pyramid forge ten feet tall with its apex sheared off, radiating ripples of firelight from above and emitting a sound from deep within its stone — a slow, deep pulse, like something breathing. A trough ran east from the forge's base, black anvils ranged along either side. And chained beneath an opening in the ceiling, runic links burning against dark crystal hide, was the dragon. It was vast and black and furious in the particular way of something powerful that has been made to hold still. Duergar ringed it in a chanting circle, voices locked to the rhythm of the runes. On a raised platform above it all, Xardorok Sunblight watched his work with the satisfaction of a man who has built something terrible and knows it. The escort moved the party through quickly, and the forge fell behind them. Imdra was in the cells. They found her, opened the lock, and put a weapon in her hand before they said much else. She looked at them with the expression of someone filing away questions for later and nodded that she was ready. The plan took shape in whispers. Grandolpha's Duergar would reposition alongside the chanting circle. Hobbins would conceal herself in the beard of one of the allied guards and ride him into range of the chanters — close enough for her most powerful magic to end as many of them as possible in a single moment. Aronious and Yin Shen would hold back and handle what remained at range. Once the chanters were clear, all fire would turn to Xardorok while the allied Duergar secured the chains. Hobbins would not move until the signal — until Polard , Mylbor , and the Shield Guardian had fought their way through the throne room and were in the forge. They waited. Then the doors at the far end of the forge burst open. Hobbins moved the moment they did. Her magic erupted through the chanting circle, two of the four Duergar dropping before the sound of it finished echoing through the cavern. Aronious took a third. The fourth still held the chain as the allied Duergar surged forward to take up the rhythm of the chant, fingers finding the runic links, voices stumbling into the pattern the dead men had left unfinished. The runes flickered. The dragon thrashed against its bonds with renewed fury. Yin Shen opened the grey bag of tricks and emptied it at Xardorok — animals surging up the platform in a snarling tide, buying seconds and forcing his attention. Then she raised Dzaan's fireball scroll and read it aloud. The explosion was effective. Xardorok turned his black crystal gauntlet toward her and hellfire tore open the floor beneath her feet from somewhere else entirely, from a plane that had no business being involved in this fight. Polard's armor blazed to life. Mylbor raised what remained of his Thunder Stick and waded in. The Shield Guardian hammered into the melee alongside Aronious's spirit reindeer, the forge filling with the noise of a battle that had been building since Easthaven burned. Hobbins sent a spell at Xardorok. He turned the gauntlet on her. The hellfire came up beneath her small body and the party watched her collapse, singed and still, to the stone floor. The fight continued around her. Aronious broke from his position and ran. He reached her and pressed his hand to her chest and called on something older than the battle around him — Sylvanas, god of nature, the same force that had touched the reindeer and the Chwinga and the herd in the snow. Healing energy passed through his palm and into her. Hobbins drew a shuddering breath and came back. Xardorok went invisible. It bought him nothing. Yin Shen had him bound with witch bolt , the arc of lightning marking him in the dark, and Aronious laid a hunter's mark on the same thread. He emerged from the shroud on the far side of the forge and threw a lever set into the wall. Ice cascaded through the hole in the ceiling in a grinding rush. He was still pulling it when the party descended on him — spell and arrow and blade converging without pause or mercy. He fell beside his lever, alone in the way that men who trade loyalty for power tend to find themselves at the end. The chains went slack. The dragon's runic bonds flickered once and failed. It raised its head, drew breath, and exhaled — not ice, but radiant light, a burst that vaporized the nearest constructs in a single sweep. Its wings snapped to their full width, filling the forge with the crack of displaced air, and with one powerful surge it launched itself upward through the hole in the ceiling and out into the open sky above Icewind Dale. The forge settled into silence around the party. Smoke drifted. Somewhere in the stone above them, the sound of wingbeats faded north. Grandolpha's Duergar held the chains that no longer bound anything.

docs.text: Session 24: Eight Hours to Easthaven The forge had gone quiet. The rest of Sunblight had not. Somewhere beyond the walls, steel was meeting steel: the sound of a fortress deciding who it belonged to, now that Xardorok lay dead beside his lever. Grandolpha offered no comment on it. In the party's presence she did nothing at all. Nobody stayed to learn how it came out. The elevator carried them up to the machinery room at the top, open to the sky. It was dusk. Far off, small against the last of the light, the dragon was flying toward Dougan's Hole , following a channel someone had carved into a stone table. Aronious worked it out the way he read terrain. Dougan's Hole, then Goodmead , then Easthaven : eight hours for the dragon. For the party, in a straight line to Easthaven, eight hours. That settled the question of rest. It did not settle the question of the two small towns in between. Goodmead had no speaker. The last one had died in a verbeeg incursion, and the seat sat empty while a handful of hopefuls reached for it, Hobbins 's father among them. Dougan's Hole had Edgra Dermoot , an old trapper woman. So it would be Edgra. Dougan's Hole would run for Easthaven and gather up Goodmead on the way. Aronious scooped Hobbins up and ran for the dogsled. She cast sending as she was carried. A dragon is coming. Eight hours. Get to Easthaven, and bring Goodmead's people with you. The answer was curt. Dougan's Hole was leaving its houses where they stood. Aronious drove and watched the sky. The dragon's flight was unsteady, and light seeped from between its plates where the Shield Guardian had hammered it, radiance leaking out of something that had been built to hold it in. The party slept in shifts on the moving sled while the dragon dropped behind them, bending away toward Dougan's Hole. Eight hours later they came up on Easthaven's gate behind the last of the evacuees, a hundred and fifty or so from the two towns, carrying what they could. The damaged walls had been patched with packed ice and snow. Behind them stood two hundred militia: a hundred and fifty in uniform, fifty who had simply turned up. Imdra left to join the commanders. Yin Shen followed her. Hobbins went to the vanguard, waved forward by a commander who remembered her from the town hall after the first Duergar trouble, and Aronious made his report. The dragon was wounded. It was about thirty minutes out. Smoke stood in the sky from the direction of Goodmead. Yin Shen found an alley with no one in it. She spoke to her sister, the one who had brought about her exile. "I know I fucked up in the past. I don't ask much from you, but please, if you can, help these people out." Snow began to fall. In a frozen puddle, the face looking back at her was not her own. It was golden and pale, there for a moment and then gone. Then the sigil of Tyr melted itself into the ice. No weapon came. No spell. But she had been heard, and she walked out of the alley carrying something she had not carried in. She was not the only one. Elsewhere in Easthaven, the other two each caught a glimpse of a figure who looked a great deal like Yin Shen: one in a shiny rock at the front of the militia, one as a shape among the stars. Imdra's writ and a deputy's standing got Aronious into a watchtower on the wall. From the top, the dragon was minutes away. Hobbins went back through Dzaan's notebook, looking for anything hidden. She found nothing. Then the wall was gone. Radiant breath shattered it, and the dragon landed in front of the militia. Yin Shen asked a commander for a healing potion. "What do I look like, the Quartermaster? Head over to the barracks and maybe you'll find something there." Imdra stayed bent over the maps. Aronious got down from the tower before it crumbled. He healed Hobbins, then caught Yin Shen at the quartermaster's door and healed her scorched arm. The quartermaster, frightened, handed over the last three healing potions in Easthaven's stores. Two went with Yin Shen, one with Aronious. One of hers would be empty before the night was over. The dragon's breath took a section of the vanguard and left nothing where it had been. The militia answered with spears, stones, and arrows, and most of it bounced off. Hobbins threw the strongest chromatic orb she had. Even with whatever had come down with the snow behind it, it went wide. She fell back behind the troops. A militiaman got his spear under one of the plates and pried. It opened. Something bright leaked out. Hobbins's next orb was lightning, and it did not miss. It blew a gaping wound in the dragon's flank. The Shield Guardian went to work on that flank with both fists, then grabbed the tail and was dragged about for its trouble. Aronious spent the last of his magic on a blessing for Yin Shen, and she took to the rooftops. Aronious lashed the dragon's helm-like jaw shut with thorn whip , and militia took hold of the vines and hauled. The next breath had nowhere to go. It went off inside, and the chardalyn around the dragon's head cracked. It nearly tore free. He held it with everything he had, including the part that had not been his an hour ago. Hobbins's second lightning orb widened the wound, and behind it sat the core: a small black hole, or a dead star. "Everyone try to hit that weak spot I just exposed." Yin Shen leapt from a rooftop onto the dragon's wing, ran up its back, and drove her short sword into a vent in its neck, pinning the head. The Shield Guardian and the reindeer kept striking. Aronious handed the vines to the militia. He drew the giant's bone longbow further than he had ever drawn it and sent an arrow clean through the core. The body began to swell. Yin Shen sprinted off its back toward a building. Hobbins spent the last magic she had on a thunderwave that drove the blast back into the dragon and away from the militia standing nearest. Hobbins was first into the crater. There was nothing in it but chardalyn fragments. Aronious found Imdra and told her what the material does to a mind with prolonged contact, a kind of necrosis, and that it should be buried rather than handled. A task force would see to the cleanup. Until then, militia would keep the townsfolk away from the site. The party found an inn. Yin Shen offered a prayer of thanks to her sister. Then they slept, all of them at once.

docs.text: Session 25: Crew Safe, Vessel in Peril Before the inn, and before anyone slept, there was the rubble. Bucket chains worked through the ruined district of Easthaven , passing snow hand to hand onto the fires. The party and Polard went through what the dragon had left, pulling out the pinned and the unconscious. Most of them, once dug free, turned out to be unhurt. Then Polard reached his own lane. The radiant breath had gone straight down it, and not one building stood. He went to his knees and wept. Hobbins asked whether the shop had been insured. Polard took out the pamphlet the party had given him, turned to the last page, and showed them the checklist. The final box was empty. "I never got it notarized." A week later the plot was twice the size it had been, Easthaven's thanks for his part in the defense. For the moment it held a tent, a sign, a freshly built workbench, and no merchandise of any kind. Polard told them he was stepping back from adventuring. A hiatus. A temporary retirement, as he put it. He meant to install a forge and train with the Easthaven blacksmith, so that whatever gear the party needed, he could supply. Aronious asked after his brother. Polard had no brother. He said he would invite him up from the south. Yin Shen bore this with open exasperation. He cried as they left, and asked them to visit often. Yin Shen said she wanted to do some shopping. She took four items to a middling jeweler's shop and asked for a private appraisal. She watched him as he looked them over. He was not obviously lowballing her. He was very interested. When he named a large sum, she did not counter. He paid with a stamped banker's note. She walked it to Easthaven's small bank and deposited the money. It had been a long day of helping Polard rebuild. The inn was giving the town's defenders complimentary crackers and cheese, and Aronious settled in front of the fire with his share and dozed off. Hobbins saw her chance and slipped out, bound for a bar across town. The bar was an old dog sled kennel: an empty shack fifteen feet across, with a hatch in the floor. Beneath the hatch, a metal spiral staircase wound down into a cavern that had no business fitting under it, packed with partygoers from more regions than Easthaven usually sees in a year. The host was a gnome wizard in the same robe and the same hat as Hobbins. He worked the room with finger guns, and out of them came confetti, balloons, and mage hands. He conjured her a clear shot. She chugged it, failed to keep it down, and vomited in the bathroom. It cleared her head. She knew him. Terence Brightbrow , party boy of the university in Waterdeep, who had bullied her for being a nerd. He denied it. "Hey, don't try and harsh my mellow. I'm here for a party for everybody." Then his finger slipped, and a streamer unfurled across the room. It read no nerds allowed . Terence bought the room a round, and every eye in the cavern began to glow blue. Hobbins left on friendly terms, with a bottle of the same white liquor under her arm. If he wanted to find her, she told him, he could ask the townsfolk. She was still on the stairs when six Easthaven guards burst into the shack above. Unpaid taxes. Cudgels only. Hobbins got into a box, pulled hay over herself, and watched through the slats. The out-of-town guests left by portal. The guards came back up with nothing but Easthaven locals, and with no explanation for why the place had been bigger a moment ago. When they were gone, she went back down. The staircase ended in the kennel's cold-storage cellar, frozen and small. Something like mighty fortress , she decided. Eighth-level conjuration, from a man whose reputation did not reach anywhere near it. She took some of the frozen dog food for the sled dogs. Aronious woke to an empty room. Nobody had seen Hobbins. Someone could point him toward where Yin Shen had been, though, and from there her footprints were as good as a map. He reached the bank square in time to watch her walk out of the bank, and she did not see him. He followed the trail backward to the jeweler: a short, stout dwarf in a monocle and a ragged top hat. It took nine gold, all told, before the dwarf brought out what she had sold him. A platinum pipe with a carved sapphire bowl. A malachite comb set with red garnets. A pile of small gemstones. A pair of black crystalline slippers. The lot was going south with the next caravan. Aronious's face did the rest of the negotiating. The jeweler, cowed, pressed a business card into his hand. On the back was a coupon: twenty-five percent off the first gold piece of any purchase over five thousand. He found her on a bench near the bank, counting gold. He sat down beside her, friendly as anything. Then he gripped her shoulder and cast alarm . She had one minute. She admitted the pieces had come from the chest in the poison room. A couple hundred gold, she said. "I almost died, okay? You trapped me in that room with the poison. I deserve this." Then she stabbed a tranquilizer dart into his neck. He was out for a few seconds. When he came to, exhausted, she was running. Thorn whip missed her once, then again. So he called his companion back as a large eagle, and it buffeted her down the street the way she had come. Hobbins arrived and dropped a hypnotic pattern into the alley. It caught them both. Aronious managed one half-hearted spank. Yin Shen, charmed, could not lie. The sale had been worth a lot. The money was in the bank. Hobbins leaned on her until she agreed to share, and Aronious and Hobbins each came away with two hundred gold. She never did say what the total was. They took the dog sleds north, toward the pull Yin Shen felt, with the Shield Guardian in tow. Aronious had stored a divine smite in it and mentioned this to no one. A long rest on the trail cleared his exhaustion. The ping in Yin Shen's skull had been there since she took the crystal. As she concentrated, the static thinned, and a gooey voice came through it. A nautiloid was down. Emergency protocols were enabled. The crew was safe, but the vessel was in peril. A psi crystal was needed at once. She told the others where they were going. They knew what a nautiloid was. Aronious and Hobbins objected, strongly. Yin Shen kept going. From a rise in the far north they looked down into a small snowy valley. The ship jutted from the snow, half grown and half built, shaped like a cephalopod and glowing. Its tentacles were as thick as tree trunks and coated in mucus that stayed liquid despite the cold. It looked as though someone had tried to bury it. The broadcast repeated. The same words, every time. Hobbins wanted no part of it and said they would stay on the sidelines. Yin Shen headed in. The snow opened beside her. Two large larval things with tentacles for faces came up out of it, and she went rigid where she stood. They dragged her under and toward the ship. Aronious's thorn whip caught her by the ankle and wrenched her free. The creatures did not turn back for her. They kept burrowing toward the nautiloid. Hobbins summoned an aberrant spirit to stand guard. It took the shape of a mind flayer. She named it Steve. Yin Shen lay face down in the snow, unable to comment.

docs.text: Session 26: Squidlings in the Snow The poison took a few minutes to wear off. Yin Shen spent them in the snow where she had fallen. Aronious and Hobbins left her to it. When she could move again, she sat for an hour and cast find familiar . What came of it was an owl. She sent it over the valley. The ship was three levels tall and half buried, with two ballistas and a long scar in the snow behind it where it had come down. Its shell was semi-translucent. There was light behind it, and things moving. The burrowers' tunnels ran fifteen or twenty feet from where they had taken her and then stopped. Of the creatures themselves, the owl found nothing. So they went down to the ship. Yin Shen went up by grappling hook to the lower outer deck. The double doors were chitin and iron, and frozen shut. Hobbins took out the sea hag's frozen eye and used it to cast detect evil and good . Five aberrations. Three in the room behind the door, one on the second level, one at the very top. The Shield Guardian vaulted onto the deck. Yin Shen melted the ice with kitsune fire, and under it was a simple mechanical latch. She looked for a trap and found none. She eased the door open. Through the gap she saw crates, and among them three small things with tentacles for faces, smaller than Polard , playing the way children play. A flesh golem was hauling boxes around them. It had been stitched together from goblins, dwarves, and reindeer. The door opened the rest of the way. The golem charged. The squidlings retreated to the back of the room. Yin Shen stepped inside with the psi crystal held out in front of her and offered peace. The squidlings fixed on the crystal. One of them scurried up the stairs. The golem was less interested. Aronious and his deer companion wounded it, and so did Hobbins's magic missile . Then it hit Yin Shen, and the blow had lightning in it. Then the wall came in. The Shield Guardian came through it and let go of the divine smite Aronious had stored there. The golem's midsection was destroyed. It went down and stayed down, though it was not dead. They left it that way. Hobbins cast comprehend languages and asked the two that remained what had happened. They answered the way toddlers do. "Ship crash. Stuck. Need help." Hobbins offered to help. The squidlings calmed, and pointed a tentacle toward the stairs, where the third had gone. On the middle deck, Yin Shen sent the owl on up to the helm. It found somewhere to hide, and nobody noticed it. Under a lattice of glowing jellyfish, a ceremorph the size of a gnome was working at a control panel. Hobbins, meanwhile, had heard Gnomish through a door. She knocked, and went in alone. Voren was a ceremorph too, gnome-sized, and he was repairing the ship. It had been a research mission, he told her. They collected creatures: two carrion crawlers, and a larger beast that tunnels. After the crash there had been no way to feed them, so they had let all three go. They answered, he said, to something called the mother brain. He insisted they were not controlled, not the way other mind flayers are. Then his scanner found a power source. It was on the other side of the wall, which was where Yin Shen was standing. "The visitors on the ship, yes, they might be able to help. I sure hope our golem hasn't done any damage to them." Hobbins asked whether he would come to the party's aid if she called by sending . "No, I don't think we can do that. We gotta get out of here. We've already caused too much trouble being stuck in this area. If someone discovers us, they'll definitely take us down." Yin Shen came in with the crystal. Voren stopped using his mouth and spoke inside their heads instead. He named it a psi crystal, and showed them the one in the ship's propulsion, burnt out. She told him hers had come from the skull of a mind flayer, in a mine. The party asked about payment. Future transport was refused. An item was not. At the helm, Dredavex , the one the owl had been watching, brought out a small chitinous chest. Inside were a pair of crystal lenses and a helmet shaped like an owl, capped with something very like a brain. Hobbins tried the lenses. They were too big for her and far from comfortable, but she could see in the dark, and she could pick out more of what she was looking at. Then she tried the helmet. It wanted attunement. She took both off again. The ceremorphs were not upset about their golem. They would rather get off the planet than dwell on it. Yin Shen handed over the psi crystal. The lenses and the owl came back the other way.

It had been a research mission, he told her. They collected creatures: two carrion crawlers, and a larger beast that tunnels. After the crash there had been no way to feed them, so they had let all three go. They answered, he said, to something called the mother brain. He insisted they were not controlled, not the way other mind flayers are. Then his scanner found a power source. It was on the other side of the wall, which was where Yin Shen was standing. "The visitors on the ship, yes, they might be able to help. I sure hope our golem hasn't done any damage to them." Hobbins asked whether he would come to the party's aid if she called by sending . "No, I don't think we can do that. We gotta get out of here. We've already caused too much trouble being stuck in this area. If someone discovers us, they'll definitely take us down." Yin Shen came in with the crystal. Voren stopped using his mouth and spoke inside their heads instead. He named it a psi crystal, and showed them the one in the ship's propulsion, burnt out. She told him hers had come from the skull of a mind flayer, in a mine. The party asked about payment. Future transport was refused. An item was not. At the helm, Dredavex , the one the owl had been watching, brought out a small chitinous chest. Inside were a pair of crystal lenses and a helmet shaped like an owl, capped with something very like a brain. Hobbins tried the lenses. They were too big for her and far from comfortable, but she could see in the dark, and she could pick out more of what she was looking at. Then she tried the helmet. It wanted attunement. She took both off again. The ceremorphs were not upset about their golem. They would rather get off the planet than dwell on it. Yin Shen handed over the psi crystal. The lenses and the owl came back the other way.
docs.title: Session 26: Squidlings in the Snow

docs.text: Session 27: A Dock Built For Giants The ceremorphs did not stay to chat. The psi crystal had hardly changed hands before they were off to mend the ship and get it into the air. Hobbins sat down with the helmet and gave it a ritual's worth of attention. A Helm of Telepathy. The lenses were Eyes of Minute Seeing. Aronious took the lenses, for the sake of seeing in the dark. Yin Shen took the owl. Voren was plain about the rest. They were bound for the Astral realm. The party could not come. After that, he did not expect anyone would be able to reach them. So the party climbed down and stood in the snow to watch. The tentacles tore free. The ship rose, and then it was a streak in the sky, and then it wasn't. They were still standing beside the hole it had left when Dzaan appeared. He was blue, and they could see the valley through him. He was still dodging the other wizards of the Arcane Brotherhood, he said. They told him about the dragon. He was astonished. Then he told them what he had been doing in Icewind Dale all along. A Netherese city, Ythryn, lay buried in the Reghed Glacier. Auril 's magic guarded the ice. Fire would not open it, and neither would a pick. A book would. On Auril's island, out in the Sea of Moving Ice, there was a tome called the Codicil of White, and in it an incantation that could split the glacier. He wanted the party to get onto the island and find it. He also wanted his professor orb back. Professor Skant, an expert on the Netherese Empire, had been stolen from him. The payoff was the city itself, and whatever magic was still lying around in it. They took the job. He marked the island on their map. The only port he knew of that far north was Revel's End, and that was a prison. The party pointed out that there was a white dragon in the way. They would ask in Easthaven instead. Yin Shen attuned to the helm on the road. By the time they reached the town hall she was in the mood to kick the door in, and did, shouting Imdra 's name. Imdra was back on duty, in a plain standard uniform. Her own gear had never come back out of Xardorok 's fortress. She had little to offer. Easthaven had no real sailors, and no water that led to the Sea of Moving Ice. What they wanted was the taverns of Targos, and a captain. A round trip, she guessed, might run fifteen gold. It was a guess. Polard 's new shop was bigger than the old one and about half finished. He had hired help. An assistant named Samantha was working the counter. The party thought the place deserved a better name, and offered one. It was a pun. Polard did not need to think about it. "Samantha, we need to change the sign immediately." So it was the Musical Empolardium. Then they asked after his brother. Polard hesitated. He stepped into the back room. A moment later a gnome came out in a different shirt and introduced himself as Finkle Shortfuse. Aronious had caught the flicker of confusion. He accepted the brother all the same. Yin Shen and Hobbins played along. Somewhere in the middle of this, Yin Shen left. Nobody saw her go. Hobbins followed her nose instead, and it led to the roof. Aronious wanted to know what she was doing up there. Helping with the sign, she said, and to prove it she tried to unhook it. The sign won. It took her off the roof with it and into a snowbank. Polard charged her one gold for the breakage, and winked at Aronious. They slept at the White Lady Inn. Aronious stored a second-level divine smite in the Shield Guardian. At dawn the writ of free passage put them on the caravan, through Bryn Shander and on to Targos. Nine and a half hours, near enough. It was about six in the evening when they got down. The tavern was called Three Flags Sailing. Yin Shen looked the room over and settled on a large man with one eye and a pipe. A captain. She asked him for passage on the Sea of Moving Ice. The whole table laughed. She might as well ring Angajuk's Bell, he told her. There was a bronze bell on the shore, the story went, and a giant whale with a wrecked ship on its back, awakened once by a frost druid to carry travelers. Ring the one and the other would come. Aronious liked the sound of that. Yin Shen said the voyage was meant to end the frost. She said they were the ones who had killed the dragon. The laughing stopped. The captain turned to his crew. It was his first mate, Dale, who talked him into it. Then came the price. The crew muddled it on purpose. Dale shook Yin Shen's hand on thirty-five gold, paid before they sailed. At the dock the quartermaster took thirty-five gold from Yin Shen and informed her that ten more would be due on return. This was more than she thought she had shaken on. The Shield Guardian went into the cargo hold. They spent a day breaking ice upriver. Then the captain got a look at the mark on Dzaan's map. There was no land there, he said. He was sure of it. He set a course for it anyway, two days out. On the first day at sea a rope came loose, and Yin Shen went to help secure it. The sail had other ideas. It flung her about for a while and set her down seasick. Aronious and Hobbins, meanwhile, helped a sailor haul in a knucklehead trout of enormous size, and the crew ate it fresh. On the second morning the cartographer could not get a fix. Yin Shen sent her owl up through the clouds to read the stars, and the course was corrected. The cold came on next. It bit, and it was wrong. They were not far enough north for it, the captain said. Then there was fog, and a great deal of it. The owl went ahead and found an island with a ruined dock. The ship came out of the fog under cliffs of ice fifty feet high. Masts stood up out of the water around them, with the ships they belonged to somewhere underneath. Ahead was the dock, carved from ice and shattered, and built for giants. The crew anchored offshore. They would not land. They would wait one day. The party wanted two. The quartermaster shoved the captain aside and named the price of the second: fifty gold. "What do you think sunk these ships? I don't see them stuck on any rocks." The haggling went on for some time. Aronious appealed to legend. It was Dale, again, who gave. Two days, the ten gold on return as agreed, and one magic item out of whatever the party found on the island. The longboat rode low with the Shield Guardian in it. On the dock an ice mephit was waving at them and jabbering. Hobbins cast comprehend languages , by ritual. The language was Auran. The mephit was Soppo. From then on she did the talking, and passed along what came back. Soppo offered to be their guide. There was plenty to see. Shipwrecks, full of goods. A recent wreck, with one survivor, who had made it as far as the shore and frozen there. A field of ice sculptures. "Soppo hasn't had visitors in a while. Again, unless you count the one who crawled ashore, though she didn't last." Hobbins asked about the orb. Soppo did not know it. She asked about the Codicil of White, and Soppo looked shocked. The lady's book, it called it. That was at Grimskalle, at the center of the island, where it was dangerous. It could take them there. A tour, fourteen hours, with Grimskalle at the end of it. They accepted. Yin Shen kept her guard up.
docs.title: Session 27: A Dock Built For Giants

docs.text: Session 3: The Prophecy at Caer-Dineval The morning after the séance brought no answers, only the lingering echo of a spirit's whisper: Caer-Dineval. By dawn, the decision was made. Yin Shen spent the early hours searching for any trace of the White Lady's presence, but found nothing. The spirit had returned to whatever cold deep claimed it. By midday, the trio had secured passage on a caravan heading north along the frozen lakeshore. When Caer-Dineval came into view, it was not welcoming. The town clung to the cliffs, and above it loomed the Caer itself — a fortress of dark stone, austere and forbidding, its towers crowned with wind-shredded banners. The party made their way to The Uphill Climb , a tavern perched northwest of the castle. Inside, the proprietor Roark served hot chowder but had no beer or spirits to offer. Yin Shen asked about the White Lady. Roark knew the ghost story but little else. When asked who ran the town, Roark told them the Speaker was Crannoc Siever , a human who kept to the Caer these days. The Caer 's entrance was barred by thick wooden doors, its guard towers rising like sentinels above. Aronious called up, requesting an audience with the Speaker. A voice rang out from above, sharp and cold, telling them the Speaker was unwell and saw no one. When Yin Shen pressed, three arrows hissed through the air in warning. One grazed Aronious's shoulder. More guards appeared at the arrow slits, bows drawn. Hobbins ' whiskers twitched with mischief. Before Yin Shen could stop her, the ferret cast her spell. High above, a guard named Henry Davis blinked, suddenly certain these travelers were trustworthy friends. He convinced his captain to let them in, and the great doors groaned open. Henry led them through cold stone corridors to the Speaker's office. The room was empty save for tax documents and other parchment scattered on the desk. Hobbins found a book — The History of Caer-Dineval — while Yin Shen asked Henry where the Speaker was. The low-ranking guard didn't know, but suggested they speak with the soothsayer, Hethyl Arkorran . Hethyl sat hunched by a brazier, her skin like parchment, one eye missing, and a peg where her right leg would have been. When asked who Hethyl and the guards were, she told them they were the Knights of the Black Sword . A name unfamiliar to the party. Hethyl had little time for idle talk and stressed to the party that Duergar are the danger. They must be stopped. Hethyl's eyes grew distant and clouded. Her voice became something older, colder, threaded with prophecy: "Hidden away, buried in the mountains, lies a fortress, a villain, a crystal machine with a dragon's heart! O, mighty wings beating and breath like the sun! Bright enough to BURN away the Rime — to burn us all if you do... not... stop..." With a final, rattling breath, Hethyl Arkorran went still. Dead. The party sent Henry to fetch the captain. When he returned with a dozen armed guards, they all tried to explain at once — their words tumbling over each other in a garbled mess. The captain's gaze moved from the dead soothsayer to the travelers, then to Henry, still smiling and standing too close to the strangers. The captain's jaw tightened. "Restrain them," he said coldly, then pointed at Henry. "And clap that traitor in irons." The guards moved forward. The moment hung frozen — a breath before the fall.

docs.text: Session 4: The Giant Beneath the Ice The moment the guards advanced, chaos erupted. Aronious bolted for the door, Hobbins clinging to his shoulders. He slipped past the first guard, boots sliding on stone, cloak snapping behind him. Another figure stepped from the shadows — robed, silent, no glint of mail beneath the fabric. A hand darted out, seizing Hobbins mid-stride. Aronious spun, eyes flashing in the torchlight. The motion carried him full circle — a low pivot, a coiled strike — and his fist crashed squarely into the stranger’s face. The impact cracked like breaking ice. The robed guard crumpled backward, sprawling across the floor in a heap of cloth and blood. Aronious caught Hobbins mid-fall, threw her back onto his shoulders, and burst through the doorway into the night. Still in the room, Yin Shen melted into shadow, slipping beneath a bed as boots thundered past. She shifted form — fur rippling into that of a fox — but the guard captain was still in the room and his search was merciless. Furniture splintered as he threw it, and when his hand closed around her tail, he lifted her high with a grunt of triumph. Without ceremony, he carried her through the frozen halls and down into the cistern — a dungeon of ice and earth where the chill stank of rot. There, Yin Shen found five others — servants of the Caer, beaten and shivering. In the frost-rimmed walls, she saw the shapes of dead guards half-buried beneath the ice, their armor bearing the Heraldry of Caer-Dineval . The living guards above had worn none. A quiet spark of defiance flared. Yin Shen whispered a word, and flame danced along her fingers. She pressed it into the permafrost, melting a narrow tunnel upward until the ceiling gave way. One by one, the prisoners climbed to freedom. Outside, Aronious and Hobbins crouched beneath the snow-drifted wall, watching. The castle was already on alert — horns had sounded when they fled through the front gate — and guards now scanned the tundra for their escape. By that stroke of fortune, no one looked inward, and Yin Shen’s group slipped unseen through the lower courtyards, making it as far as the kennels before the hounds caught their scent. Barking erupted. Shouts followed. The alarm spread like wildfire. From their hiding place beyond the walls, Aronious spotted the movement. “There!” he hissed. Together, he and Hobbins sprinted for the gate. As the portcullis began to drop, they threw their weight against it, Hobbins’ small claws scraping for purchase. Yin Shen and the prisoners surged through the narrowing gap. Aronious wedged his bow into the iron grate, holding it just long enough for the last of them to tumble free. With one final shove, the gate slammed shut behind them. Breathless but alive, the group hurried down the snow-slick hill to The Uphill Climb in the town below. There, amid the warmth of the hearth and the smell of ale and stew, they nursed their bruises and shared what little they had learned of the Caer’s strange garrison. By morning, the road east called. Aronious and Hobbins growing increasingly concerned for the missing fishermen that awaited their rescue in Easthaven . The trio took their leave, taking a caravan across the endless white until the lights of the town vanished behind them. On the ice of Lac Dinneshere , they found the fishermen’s trail: a patch of open water, an abandoned boat, and a cliffside pocked with dark cave mouths. The smallest opened directly onto the frozen lake, its floor a smooth, glassy riverbed. The higher caves were steep and treacherous, so they took the safer path within. The tunnel forked — one branch descending deeper into the ice, the other rising along a rocky ledge. They chose the higher way, and it led to a vast chamber heavy with silence and the stench of old death. In its center slumped a giant’s skeleton, armor fused to its bones, axe frozen in its grasp. When they stepped closer, the corpse stirred. What followed was battle in the dark. Yin Shen’s blades flashed in starlight. Hobbins darted between the giant’s ribs, hurling bursts of fire from Aronious’s bow. The creature tore free one arm, swinging its axe like a falling tree. Aronious’s thorn whip lashed around the haft, binding it fast. The ferret hurled her last vial of ink, blotting out one of the giant’s glowing eyes; Yin Shen followed, leaping to its skull and forcing a waterskin into the other. With a final, soul-shaking howl, the light died. The bones cracked, crumbled, and fell. A streak of blue fire shot from the ruin, vanishing through the cave mouth and into the storm beyond. When the echoes faded, the heroes stood alone in the stillness — three figures in the dark, their breath misting in victory and awe.
docs.title: Session 4: The Giant Beneath the Ice
